questions.question: What is model cascading / model routing as a cost-reduction primitive?
options: Running the same model on multiple hardware configurations and picking the fastest response
A dynamic broker that sends simple queries to a cheap model and escalates complex ones to a frontier model
Caching model weights across replicas to avoid redundant downloads
Splitting long prompts across multiple models in parallel and merging outputs
questions.explanation: Model routing (cascading) evaluates each request and routes it to the cheapest model capable of meeting quality requirements. Simple queries go cheap; complex queries escalate to frontier. Production case studies show 20-60% cost reduction at iso-quality.

questions.question: The lesson names four routing signals. Which of these is NOT one of the four?
options: Task classification (task type)
Prompt token length
Embedding similarity to known-hard query set
User subscription tier
questions.explanation: The four routing signals are: task classification, prompt length, embedding similarity to a known-hard set, and self-confidence from a first-pass cheap model. User subscription tier is a business rule, not one of the four ML-based routing signals.

questions.question: What is cheap-model drift and why is it dangerous?
options: The cheap model's weights drift over time due to provider fine-tuning changes
Too much traffic routes to the cheap model, quality drops 3-5% on reasoning tasks, and nobody notices for a quarter
The cheap model becomes more expensive over time as providers increase prices
The router itself degrades as the embedding model used for routing ages out of distribution
questions.explanation: Cheap-model drift: the router pushes 40%+ of traffic to a weaker model, quality drops 3-5% on reasoning tasks — subtle enough to miss in aggregate metrics, but visible to users. The fix is gating routes by online quality metrics (LLM-judge on 5% sample, user thumbs-down rate) not just offline evals.

questions.question: What was the approximate price of a GPT-4-class token in 2022 versus 2026?
options: $5/M in 2022 vs $2/M in 2026 (2.5x drop)
$20/M in 2022 vs ~$0.40/M in 2026 (~10x per year drop)
questions.explanation: The lesson cites ~$20/M tokens for GPT-4-class in late 2022 dropping to ~$0.40/M in 2026 — approximately 10x per year aggregate. Most of the drop came from better serving stacks, not hardware. Routing is how teams convert that drop into margin.

questions.question: What is the latency impact of cascading, and what percentage of traffic typically escalates to the frontier model?
options: ~1x (no overhead); ~50% escalation
~1.2x median latency; ~2x on escalated requests; typically ~10% escalation
~3x median latency; ~5x on escalated requests; typically ~30% escalation
Latency is unchanged; only cost changes
questions.explanation: The lesson states cascade adds ~1.2x median latency (cheap model first pass) with ~2x latency on the ~10% of requests that escalate to the frontier model. This is the acceptable overhead for 20-60% cost savings.

questions.question: Which online metric specifically monitors whether the cascade is over-routing to the cheap model?
options: GPU utilization per route
Escalation rate: if it exceeds 30%, the cheap model is being over-routed
Token cost per request per route
P99 TTFT per route
questions.explanation: The lesson names escalation rate as the key drift signal: if the cheap model is being escalated more than ~30% of the time, it means the router is sending traffic to the cheap tier that it cannot handle. This is over-routing.
